source: Cambodia Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries (MAFF), "ប្រព័ន្ធវប្បកម្មដំណាំស្រូវ តាមគោលការណ៍ធម្មជាតិ (ប.វ.ស)" [System of Rice Intensification Following Natural Principles / SRI], 14-page Khmer-language handout/booklet, undated, no author or elibrary URL visible on any page (footer reads "កំរណ៉ការអភិវ័ទ្ធន៍វិស្ស័យកសិកម្ម ខែត្តកំពងចាម" = "Agricultural Extension/Skills Development Office, Kampong Cham province")
text:
The source document includes a two-column comparison table contrasting conventional/traditional rice practice against SRI practice. Because the printed table is dense and the visual alignment between the two columns was not fully certain on every row, the content below is given as a general paired comparison by theme rather than a claimed exact row-by-row transcription (noted here per the source's own visual review).

Seed and nursery bed: Traditional practice does not carefully select good/full seed grains for sowing, keeps a lot of standing water in the nursery bed, and sows seed densely, which produces thin/weak seedlings. SRI practice selects good quality, full seed; prepares a raised, well-drained nursery bed; and sows thinly (a figure of about 0.5 kg per 5 m2 of bed appears in this part of the source).

Transplanting age and method: Traditional practice pulls seedlings roughly, damaging roots, ties them into bundles, and may leave them overnight or longer before transplanting seedlings that are commonly over one month old, mixing strong and weak seedlings together at planting. SRI practice pulls only healthy seedlings and transplants immediately, using seedlings younger than 15 days, with 1-2 seedlings per hill.

Row/hill spacing: both columns of the source table reference a spacing figure of about 25-40 cm between hills, adjusted according to soil fertility; the source did not make clear whether this spacing differs between the traditional and SRI columns or is a shared reference figure, so it is recorded here as a shared data point rather than attributed uniquely to either practice.

Water management: Traditional practice keeps continuous standing water in the field throughout the crop. SRI practice avoids continuous deep flooding, keeping water shallow or the soil only moist, with more deliberate wetting/drying management.

Weeding: Traditional practice weeds infrequently and not on a fixed schedule. SRI practice weeds frequently and on a regular schedule.

Fertilizer: Traditional practice relies less on natural/organic fertilizer such as compost, using more chemical fertilizer. SRI practice emphasizes natural fertilizer, especially compost.

Harvest timing: both columns reference doing land/harvest work at the correct, well-judged time, though the exact contrast intended between the two columns on this final row was not fully legible.
